analysis.one_liner: Pays kidney donors $50,000 in tax credits to shrink the transplant waiting list.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025; it had 18 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give anyone who donates a kidney to a stranger — not to a specific person they know — a refundable tax credit of $10,000 a year for five years, $50,000 total, even if they owe little or no income tax. If the donor dies during those five years, the rest of the $50,000 is paid out at once. The bill also changes the 1984 law banning payment for organs so the credit doesn't count as illegal payment. Roughly 90,000 Americans sit on the kidney waiting list, many for years on dialysis, because there aren't enough donated kidneys; the idea is that a large payment would persuade more healthy people to donate. The bill was introduced on August 2, 2024, sent to two committees, and referred to a health subcommittee on December 17 — but no committee ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People waiting for a kidney transplant, whose odds improve if more healthy people donate to strangers; living donors, who receive $50,000 over five years; and their families, since a working transplant ends years of dialysis treatments.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit of $10,000 per year for five years — $50,000 total — for anyone who donates a kidney to an anonymous stranger, refundable meaning donors receive it even if they owe little or no federal income tax.
If a donor dies during the five-year period, the family receives the remainder of the $50,000 immediately.
Amends the National Organ Transplant Act, the 1984 law that bans paying people for organs, so that this specific credit is not treated as illegal 'valuable consideration.'
The credit applies to kidneys removed after December 31, 2024, and no credit is allowed for donations after December 31, 2034, making it a ten-year program.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, at roughly $50,000 per donor over five years; the Congressional Budget Office never scored the bill, so the total cost was never published.

drawbacks.text: The bill effectively creates an exception to the decades-old American ban on paying people for body parts: to make the credit legal, it amends the National Organ Transplant Act so the $50,000 doesn't count as 'valuable consideration' for a kidney.

Critics of paying organ donors have long argued that cash payments fall hardest on people in financial distress, who may feel pressure to undergo major surgery and to downplay health risks in screening, and that a $50,000 credit is designed to be persuasive precisely to lower-income people.

Because the bill is refundable, every donor draws the full $50,000 regardless of income, and the bill carries no cost estimate, so taxpayers would be committing to an unpriced entitlement for ten years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential payoff is large: a transplant ends years of dialysis and the national waitlist is long, while a single extra donor can set off a chain of matched donations. The design is also unproven — no one knows how many donors $50,000 would produce, the price tag was never estimated, and paying for body parts raises real safety and fairness concerns that the bill addresses only by carving itself out of the organ-sale ban. A fair reading is that the benefit could be substantial but the bill was a first sketch, not a finished law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced late in the session, sent to two committees, referred to a health subcommittee in mid-December, and never received a vote of any kind before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Nicole Malliotakis introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, joined by Representatives Josh Harder, Don Bacon, and Joe Neguse — a Republican sponsor with Democratic cosponsors from the start.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced.
On December 17, 2024, with the Congress five weeks from ending, the bill was referred to the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means — one step below a full committee vote.
Eighteen members cosponsored the bill: 13 of the 216 House Democrats and 5 of the 224 House Republicans.
No committee, subcommittee, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dialysis providers keep their patient base, since no additional living-donor transplants will occur through this program; the roughly 90,000 Americans waiting for a kidney remain on the list. Taxpayers avoided an uncosted new credit.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — a Republican sponsor with two Democratic original cosponsors — and the 18 cosponsors split 13 Democrats to 5 Republicans; no one voted against it because it never came to a vote.

industries.note: Every living-donor transplant takes a patient off dialysis, the main revenue source of large dialysis chains; a wave of new donations would shrink their patient census. Nothing in the record shows these companies took a position, but their financial interest in this bill ran against the patients it would help.
More donated kidneys means more transplant operations to perform and more referral volume. Their interest runs alongside patients waiting for organs.
